candidates.title: Effectiveness of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) with Batfish for LLM-generated vendor CLI configurations
candidates.research_question: Does a generate–verify–repair pipeline that uses an LLM for config generation, Batfish as a deterministic verifier, and an automated repair loop measurably reduce semantic/safety verification failures compared to plain LLM generation for vendor-specific network configuration tasks?
hypotheses: A GVR pipeline that interposes Batfish between generation and application will produce a lower rate of verifier-detected semantic/safety failures than direct LLM outputs.

The GVR pipeline will require a bounded number of automated repair iterations for the majority of tasks (<5 iterations median) while keeping overall end-to-end latency within an operationally plausible bound compared to manual workflows.
candidates.proposed_design: Controlled paired experiment using a public NetOps task set (derived from NetConfEval-like tasks and vendor CLI snippets). For each intent: (1) generate configuration using an LLM baseline; (2) run Batfish verifier on the generated config; (3) if verifier fails, invoke an automated repair procedure (LLM prompted with verifier counterexample + constraints) up to a fixed retry budget. Record verifier outcomes, repair iterations, and latencies. Run across multiple vendor CLIs (Cisco-like, Juniper-like) using open datasets and synthetic topologies. Use fixed seeds and frozen prompts; preregister retry budget and stopping rules.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task records: initial LLM output, Batfish pass/fail, repair iteration count, final Batfish pass/fail, time per step, generated config diffs, and classification of failure modes (syntax, policy violation, reachability). Aggregate counts of initial failures, final failures after repair, median repair iterations, and latency distributions.
candidates.primary_outcome: Relative reduction in verifier-detected failures: proportion of tasks passing Batfish after GVR versus passing on initial LLM output (paired proportion difference).
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute paired proportions of verifier pass before vs after GVR; test with McNemar's or paired proportion test and report 95% CIs. Report median and IQR of repair iterations and end-to-end latency; compare latency distributions with Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Perform failure-mode stratified analyses (syntax vs semantic vs reachability). Report effect sizes and bootstrapped CIs. Predefine significance threshold and adjust for multiple comparisons if testing across vendors.
risks: Batfish or verifier may have false negatives (miss real violations) producing false safety signals.
Repair loop may oscillate or fail to converge for certain intents increasing latency beyond acceptable bounds.
Vendor-specific constructs may be underrepresented in public datasets, reducing generalizability.
LLM prompt sensitivity could drive brittle outcomes if prompts are not robustly validated.

candidates.title: Quantifying verifier coverage versus latency and throughput trade-offs when integrating Batfish into high-throughput LLM NetOps agent loops
candidates.research_question: What are the empirical trade-offs between verifier strictness/coverage, false-negative acceptance, and end-to-end throughput/latency when integrating Batfish-style verification into a high-throughput LLM-driven NetOps agent pipeline?
hypotheses: Increasing verifier strictness (more checks, deeper path analyses) will reduce accepted incorrect configurations but will increase per-task verification latency and reduce throughput.

Caching and incremental verification strategies will recover a portion of throughput loss while maintaining most of the verifier's reduction in false-accepts compared to naïve always-on deep verification.
candidates.proposed_design: Instrumented throughput experiment: generate a high-volume stream of NetOps intents synthesized from public topologies and NetConfEval-like tasks. Configure multiple verifier modes (light, medium, deep) representing increasing check sets and depth. For each mode, measure: verifier latency, end-to-end throughput (intents/sec), false-negative acceptance rate (cases where final applied config violates ground-truth property despite verifier pass) using an external oracle/simulator, and cost (CPU-time). Evaluate caching/incremental verification variants. All runs use deterministic seeds and frozen prompts; preregister workload size and oracle definitions.
candidates.expected_data: Per-mode records: verifier latency distribution, throughput (intents/sec), false-negative rate against oracle, CPU cost, cache hit rates for incremental modes, and distribution of verification times over tasks.
candidates.primary_outcome: Trade-off curve (Pareto frontier) mapping false-negative acceptance rate against end-to-end throughput and median latency for each verifier mode and caching strategy.
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate and visualize false-negative rate versus throughput for each verifier mode. Use regression to quantify the effect of verifier depth on latency and false-negative rate. Use bootstrapped CIs for rates. Perform pairwise comparisons of caching vs non-caching using paired tests on throughput and false-negative rates. Report cost per avoided false accept (CPU-time per unit reduction in false-negative rate).
risks: Oracle/simulator used to label false negatives may be incomplete, biasing false-negative estimates.
Synthetic high-throughput workload may not capture real-world request correlations or worst-case topologies.
Verifier resource consumption could be prohibitive at scale, limiting the experimental envelope.
Caching/incremental strategies may introduce statefulness that complicates reproducibility.

candidates.title: Effectiveness of constrained-decoding techniques to prevent semantic constraint violations in vendor-specific network configuration generation
candidates.research_question: How effective are constrained-decoding techniques (grammar- or token-constraint enforcement) at preventing semantic and policy constraint violations in LLM-generated vendor-specific CLI configurations compared to unconstrained generation and RAG+verifier pipelines?
hypotheses: Constrained decoding will reduce the rate of semantic constraint violations (e.g., invalid CLI sequences, interface mismatches) relative to unconstrained LLM outputs.

Constrained decoding will trade off flexibility, producing fewer creative solutions and potentially yielding more syntax-level rejections or reduced applicability in edge-case intents compared to RAG+verifier approaches.
candidates.proposed_design: Implement constrained-decoding options: (A) grammar-based token constraint enforcement derived from vendor CLI grammars, and (B) token-whitelisting with dynamic slot filling. Compare three pipelines on the same public intent set: unconstrained LLM generation, constrained decoding, and RAG+verifier (LLM with retrieval + Batfish). Measure semantic violations, syntactic parse errors, functional applicability, and generation coverage. Use frozen prompts and grammar artifacts; preregister metrics and exclusion rules.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task outcomes: whether output conforms to grammar, whether verifier (when applied) reports semantic violations, coverage (fraction of tasks with usable config), generation success/failure codes, and example-level diagnostics showing trade-offs.
candidates.primary_outcome: Percent reduction in semantic constraint violations (as judged by verifier or grammar-based checker) for constrained decoding versus unconstrained baseline.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare violation rates across methods with paired proportion tests; report coverage differences with McNemar's test. Analyze cases of reduced applicability qualitatively and quantify increases in parse/syntax failures. Use subgroup analyses per vendor CLI complexity and intent type. Report calibration of constrained decoder (false blocks vs true prevention).
risks: Constructing accurate vendor grammars from public data may be incomplete, causing false-positive blocking of valid configs.
Constrained decoding could reduce coverage for novel valid configurations, lowering practical utility.
Implementation complexity for token-level constraints may limit real-time applicability.
Comparisons to RAG+verifier may favor one approach depending on retrieval/index freshness and verifier coverage.

candidates.title: Optimizing automated acceptance thresholds combining model confidence and verifier signals to minimize false-accepts under an automated-apply policy
candidates.research_question: Given available signals (LLM confidence/calibration, verifier pass/fail, repair history), what automated-apply acceptance thresholds achieve the best trade-off between operational coverage (fraction of intents auto-applied) and false-accept risk (ratio of incorrectly accepted configs) in a simulated operational policy environment?
hypotheses: Policies that require both a verifier pass and a calibrated high model confidence will yield a lower false-accept rate for a given auto-apply coverage than policies that rely on model confidence alone.
Inclusion of repair-history signals (e.g., number of repair iterations, presence of counterexamples) will further reduce false-accepts at modest cost to auto-apply coverage.
Well-calibrated confidence improves threshold reliability; poor calibration substantially degrades policy performance.
candidates.proposed_design: Simulated policy sweep experiment using a labeled dataset of intents with ground-truth correctness. Define simulated automated-apply policies parameterized by thresholds on model confidence, verifier pass requirement, and maximum allowed repair iterations. For each policy, compute auto-apply coverage and false-accept rate against ground truth. Evaluate impact of confidence calibration (apply temperature scaling vs uncalibrated). Use deterministic seeds and preregister cost function (trade-off) for selecting operational thresholds.
candidates.expected_data: For each policy threshold: auto-apply coverage, false-accept rate, confusion matrices, distribution of repair iterations among auto-applied cases, and calibrated vs uncalibrated performance comparisons. Pareto frontiers across policy families.
candidates.primary_outcome: Pareto frontier expressing minimal false-accept rate achievable at each level of auto-apply coverage for sets of policies (confidence-only, verifier+confidence, verifier+confidence+repair-history).
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute ROC-like curves mapping coverage to false-accept rate for each policy family. Use bootstrapped CIs for rates. Quantify calibration impact by comparing Brier score and threshold stability before/after temperature scaling. Identify policy thresholds minimizing a preregistered loss (weighted sum of false-accept rate and unreached auto-apply coverage). Perform sensitivity analyses to oracle labeling noise.
risks: Simulated policy and oracle may not reflect human decision-making or real operational costs, limiting external validity.
Model confidence may be poorly calibrated in practice, making real-world thresholds brittle.
Verifier blind spots can make verifier pass a noisy signal, producing overconfident auto-apply decisions.
Cost weighting in threshold selection may be organization-specific and require domain tuning.
